problem:
Meridian Bank processes 20,000 transactions in a day across its payment channels. The morning reconciliation shows 500 transactions unmatched between the ledger and the clearing reports. At an average of INR 8,000 per transaction, the unmatched population represents an illustrative exposure of INR 40 lakh, calculated as 500 multiplied by INR 8,000. The finance director wants to know whether the bank has lost INR 40 lakh, and the operations manager wants to know how many of the 500 are real breaks and how many are timing differences.

The headline number is a starting point, not a conclusion. An unmatched item may be a payment that cleared a day late, a fee that was never disclosed, a duplicate posting, or a genuine missing payment. The learner must quantify the gap honestly, separate timing differences from true breaks, validate the facts at transaction level, and explain the exposure without overstating it.
solution:
Quantify in layers, and never present an illustrative figure as a confirmed loss. First, state the population clearly: 20,000 transactions processed, 500 unmatched, an unmatched rate of 2.5 percent, and an illustrative exposure of INR 40 lakh based on 500 multiplied by an average of INR 8,000. State that the average is an assumption and that the real exposure must be calculated from the actual amounts of the unmatched items.

Second, classify every unmatched item by cause. Timing differences are items that will match when a late statement or a next-day clearing report arrives. Fee and foreign exchange differences are items where the settled amount differs for an explained reason. Duplicates are items posted twice. True breaks are items with no matching record on the other side, an unexplained amount difference, or a missing reference. Each class needs a different action, a different owner and a different ageing rule.

Third, validate at transaction level. Reconcile using stable identifiers, amount, currency, date and participant references, and trace a sample of items from the ledger to the clearing report and back. Check control totals at each stage: record counts, gross amounts and net amounts. Fourth, act on the results: clear timing differences when their counterpart arrives, post explained differences only under approved accounting rules, reverse duplicates once, and investigate true breaks with a named owner and a deadline. Report the residual unexplained exposure separately from the illustrative total, and track the unmatched rate daily so a rising trend is caught early.

decision.question: Meridian Bank has 500 unmatched transactions out of 20,000, averaging INR 8,000 each, an illustrative exposure of INR 40 lakh. The finance director asks whether the bank has lost INR 40 lakh. What is the correct response?

options.label: A
options.detail: Write off the INR 40 lakh so reconciliation balances.

options.label: B
options.detail: No. Report the illustrative exposure, then classify each unmatched item as a timing difference, a fee or foreign exchange difference, a duplicate or an error, and validate at transaction level before stating any loss.

options.label: C
options.detail: Yes, report a INR 40 lakh loss immediately.

options.label: D
options.detail: Ignore the 500 because they are only 2.5 percent of the total.

decisionRationale: Option B is correct because the INR 40 lakh is the value of the unmatched population, not a proven loss. Only transaction-level classification can say how much is timing, how much is explained, and how much is a real break. Option C overstates an unproven loss. Option D dismisses a material control signal. Option A hides the break instead of investigating it.

steps.title: Processes 20,000 transactions and records each with its references
Posts the ledger entries for the day
Matches ledger entries to clearing records by reference, amount, currency and date
Reports 500 unmatched items and calculates the illustrative exposure
Classifies each unmatched item as timing, fee, duplicate or true break
Traces a sample at transaction level and validates the classification
Posts approved corrections, reports the residual unexplained exposure, and tracks the unmatched rate daily

happy: Reconciliation matches 19,500 transactions automatically. Of the 500 unmatched, most prove to be timing differences that match when the next clearing report arrives, a small number are explained fee differences, and only a handful are true breaks. Each true break is investigated, corrected once, and the residual unexplained exposure is reported as a small, specific figure with named owners, not as the illustrative INR 40 lakh.

negative.title: Late statement
negative.detail: The clearing report arrives late, so items appear unmatched at the morning run. Classify them as timing differences, hold them for the next report, and confirm they match before closing them.

negative.title: Unexplained short settlement
negative.detail: The settled amount is less than expected with no disclosed fee. Classify as a true break, investigate with the clearing participant, and do not write it off without policy approval.

negative.title: Duplicate posting
negative.detail: A payment is posted twice in the ledger. Identify the duplicate by reference and amount, reverse one posting once, and fix the control that allowed the duplicate.

negative.title: Report totals wrong, source correct
negative.detail: Operational screens show correct transactions but the management report totals are wrong. Trace lineage from source through extraction, transformation and aggregation, reconcile control totals at each stage, and fix the stage that caused the variance.

technical: Define reconciliation keys explicitly: instruction ID, end-to-end ID, transaction reference, amount, currency, value date and participant reference, with tolerances for fees and foreign exchange. Reconcile at record count, gross amount and net amount, and keep control totals at each stage of any reporting pipeline so a variance can be located. Classify breaks with a controlled set of categories, ageing rules and owners, and never auto-write off an unexplained item. Keep the original ledger entry and clearing record for every break, and record the investigation, the decision and the correction against the same case. Handle partial batches by giving each transaction an independent outcome, so a valid item is not held back by a failed one. Track the unmatched rate, the aged break count and the residual exposure as daily control measures.

accounting: Debit and credit entries must match clearing reports for amount, currency and value date. Timing differences need no accounting correction, only monitoring until their counterpart arrives. Explained fee and foreign exchange differences are posted as separate lines under approved rules. Duplicate postings are reversed once, with the original reference and a documented reason. True breaks sit on a reconciliation worklist with an owner, an age and a service level, and no break is written off without policy approval. The illustrative INR 40 lakh exposure is reported as illustrative, and the residual unexplained exposure is reported separately once classification is complete. Daily reporting covers the unmatched count, the unmatched rate, aged breaks and residual exposure.

questions.question: 500 unmatched transactions average INR 8,000 each. What is the illustrative exposure?
questions.explanation: 500 multiplied by INR 8,000 equals INR 40,00,000, which is INR 40 lakh. It is illustrative until validated at transaction level.

questions.question: What is the difference between a timing difference and a true break?
options: A timing difference is always a loss.
A true break always matches the next day.
A timing difference will match when a late report arrives; a true break has no matching record or an unexplained difference.
questions.explanation: Timing differences resolve with time and the missing counterpart. True breaks need investigation and correction.

questions.question: Why must the INR 40 lakh not be reported as a loss?
options: Because it is the value of the unmatched population based on an average, not a proven loss, and most items may be timing or explained differences.
Because finance has not approved it.
questions.explanation: Only transaction-level classification can establish how much, if anything, is actually lost.

questions.question: A settlement is short with no disclosed fee. What should happen?
options: Classify it as a true break, investigate, and do not write it off without policy approval.
questions.explanation: An unexplained short settlement is a break. It needs investigation and approved treatment, never an automatic write-off.
